newsitem.title: UK: Top-level probe launched into British budget leak.
newsitem.headline: Top-level probe launched into British budget leak.

text.p: The British government has launched a top-level probe into an unprecedented leak of closely-guarded budget details to a tabloid newspaper.
Prime Minister John Major's office confirmed on Tuesday that the 36 budget documents which found their way to the editor of The Daily Mirror were genuine.
The paper called the leaks "the shambles of the decade," but did not print the documents, saying publication would have brought chaos to international financial markets.
But news of their contents were broadly hinted at in a huge embarrassment for Major's government, already rocked by a row over Europe last weekend.
The breach of security around the budget, normally eagerly awaited by ordinary taxpayers and financial market dealers, will cost the culprit dear if found.
The inquiry, which newsapers said would be led by the MI5 intelligence agency, will focus on civil servants, although the plant where the releases were printed will also be probed.

The most notorious leak in British budget history was in 1947 when the Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer, Hugh Dalton, gave budget details to a journalist as he headed into the House of Commons chamber to make his speech.

Dalton believed it was too late to get into print. But the details -- a penny on a pint of beer and a tax on dog racing -- were phoned to one of London's evening papers and appeared on the streets before Dalton reached that point in his speech.
Dalton, cuttingly described by the then Prime Minister Clement Attlee as "a perfect ass," resigned the next day.

The last major case of someone using budget secrets for personal advantage was in 1936, when Colonial Secretary Jimmy Thomas, a member of the cabinet, could not resist a play on words as he played golf with a friend from the City of London.
His remark, "Tee up," led to an unusual rush to take out insurance policies at Lloyd's against any tea duty rises.
The Chancellor announced the rise. An inquiry pointed the finger at Thomas, who quit, as did fellow member of parliament Alfred Butt, who used the information for "personal gain".
Since then, security has been tightened dramatically.

In a jokey reference to the traditional Indian curtain used to protect women from the sight of strangers, treasury ministers and officials go into "purdah" for the two months before the statement, strictly avoiding comment on any budget matters.
But there have still been occasional upsets.

Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher was accused of giving away budget secrets when in 1981 she briefed political journalists from four newspapers, all of whom correctly predicted no rise in the basic rate of income tax.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Nigel Lawson, himself a former Financial Times journalist, was stunned when some details of his first budget were leaked to the Guardian newspaper in 1984.
Other countries are less rigorous, or less bothered.
In Italy, leaks are common in the weeks preceeding the official budget. The reports are mainly based on government and parliamentary sources although they are not always accurate.
In Germany, budget secrecy is not really an issue. Details of finance minister Theo Waigel's 1997 budget were released in advance of his first parliamentary budget speech back in July.

The culprit's fate could mirror that of a civil servant sacked and imprisoned after leaking information about nuclear missiles. She was caught because of special marks on the photocopier, but most leakers escape identification.
